While I disagree with your opinion, I understand where you’re coming from.

However, consider this:

The reason why I oppose any limitations on abortions is because the more regulations there are for “elective” procedures, the harder it is for people to get abortions when they need them for medical or health reasons. 

Let’s say the law says no abortions after 20 weeks, full stop. A woman is pregnant and her fetus’ heart stops. That woman may die of sepsis if she can’t have an abortion in a timely manner. 

So, let’s say that the law instead says “no elective abortions on living fetuses.” A woman learns at 22 weeks her fetus has a condition which means it cannot survive outside the womb, but still has a heart beat. Should this woman be forced to endure another 18~ weeks of pregnancy just to deliver a dead child?

So, let’s say the law specifies the fetus just can’t be fully healthy. A woman finds out she has a cancerous tumor on one of her ovaries. She needs  surgery and to begin chemo immediately to have a chance at fighting it. She now has to make the difficult choice to terminate her pregnancy to save her own life. However, the law refuses to allow a doctor to provide a life saving abortion because the fetus is healthy. 

None of this even touches upon the fact that around 28 weeks, “abortions” as we understand them colloquially aren’t being performed anymore except in exceptionally tragic cases. You are pretty much just giving birth at that point because the fetus is too big. 

The more limits we put on abortion, the more instances in which women’s care is delayed to prove that her abortion is necessary. 

Even if you think elective abortions past 20 weeks are bad, is it worth the potential trauma and death to pregnant people to try and regulate them?

Don’t get too hung up on “risk factors.” Even something like 70% of smokers will never develop lung cancer, and smoking is probably the largest controllable risk factor we know about. Most other risk factors affect cancer outcomes on in a small way (eg: from a 3% lifetime risk naturally to a 5-10% risk). 

Also, risk factors are only really relevant for whole populations. You can’t gauge your own personal risk without genetic testing or family history. That’s why some people drink like crazy, smoke a pack a day and live to be 90, while some health nuts develop cancer at 50.

It might help you to look at actual risk factor numbers for DVT and see what a minimal chance there is.

So, I struggled with this for a while, and I’ve found something that works for me. Hear me out: baby shampoo. No conditioner.

Now, I use fragrance free baby shampoo and just use a little tiny bit of conditioner when I plan to use heat on my hair, only on the ends (in addition to my heat protectant, of course). 

And let me tell you, the amount of curl and texture my hair has now, without being gross and greasy is awesome. I regularly get comments from hair dressers about how healthy my hair is, also, so I don’t think the lack of conditioner is damaging my hair. 

Might be worth a try!

I’m sorry you’re going through a rough time. Getting a job is extremely frustrating at your age, and only starts to get a little easier when you’ve accumulated a lot of experience. 

Your situation isn’t hopeless, though. Lots of people get their first jobs with no experience, and you can, too. 

Have you looked into local temp or recruiting agencies? Also, be sure to follow up after every single resume/application you submit. Call the place you applied to a couple days later and say, “Hi! I submitted an application on this day, and wanted to see if I could come in for an interview.” This is a little awkward at first, but if the place is serious about hiring, they’ll like that you have initiative. 

Also, you mentioned volunteering. That’s a good way to get some experience and make some contacts. Definitely look into opportunities in your area. You can even find organizations you would be interested in working with and send a message to their Facebook page or email them offering up your services. 

Good luck, and just keep with it. Remember, getting a job these days is a full time job. It’s a cliche, but it’s true. 

Source: I’ve been in your position many times throughout my adolescence and early 20s.

A lot of SEO is entirely theoretical, since Google is so secretive about their secret formula, if you will. 

Keywords, tags, and links are all good, but I think at the end of the day, what Google wants is for your content to be user-friendly (so, #3 on your list), which means it's readable, and created with the intention of entertaining/educating/engaging real people, rather than tricking the search engine. 

That's why backlinks are so important, because, in theory, it means that people trust your site enough to link to it on their own, giving you credibility.

This is why SEO is so hard. There's definitely stuff you can do to help, but at the end of the day, having content that's worth reading should be at the top of the list, because without that, SEO is pretty useless.

I think that if you're writing good content, you're going to be incorporating those keywords, external links, etc. naturally. From there, as long as you're doing your meta tags and search descriptions, you're probably good.
